newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa markets cheer forex control milestone.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa markets cheer forex control milestone.

text.p: South Africa's financial markets cheered the milestone relaxation of foreign exchange controls on individuals on Tuesday as the rand shrugged off initial jitters to trade stronger on the day.

After opening weaker, the rand steadily regained its composure by midday and moved firmer in the afternoon, helping long bond yields to fresh 16-month lows and prodding the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's industrial index to fresh highs.
Analysts described the easing of foreign exchange controls, which allows South African residents to invest up to 200,000 rand offshore for the first time since 1961, as a non-event.
"Its been exceptionally quiet. A lot of enquiries but a non-event," said Autrey Wilke, general manager of international treasury trading at Absa Bank.

"It's gone pretty much according to plan as called by the authorities," added UAL Merchant Bank Treasury senior general manager Peter Lane. "On balance all the markets have reacted neutral to positive."
Foreign exchange dealers said that both local and offshore market players who had accumulated dollars in anticipation of demand had turned sellers, after the buying failed to materialise.

That helped the rand strengthen two cents from its weakest level of 4.5425 reached earlier in the day. In mid-afternoon trade it was trading at 4.5245/5275 against the dollar from 4.5280/5310 late on Monday.
"Everyone is selling the dollars they had in anticipation of the demand which has not materialised," one rand trader said.
On the bond market, the yield on the benchmark R150 loan was last yielding 14.235 percent from 14.36 percent previously, while the industrial index was up 16 points to 8,807.

The markets had been on edge before Tuesday on concerns that the country faced an exodus of capital from the country. Some analysts put the amount that could leave the country post-July 1 at 15 billion rand.
But those fears were soothed last week when the Reserve Bank said it had access to a war chest of 38 billion rand of reserves and credit lines which it could use to smooth market volatility.
The central bank has predicted that between three and five billion rand will leave the country, although analysts believe the first signs of outflows will only be seen in the weeks ahead.

"A lot of commentators have been saying don't rush out and buy foreign currency just for the sake of it and I think people have been very cautious," Peter Wylie, general manager of Societe Generale Treasury said.
"We won't see the effects for maybe the next few weeks. People will sit back and think about it and then come in," Wylie added.

Analysts noted, however, that any outflows would be countered by continuing offshore investment in South African bonds and equities whose recent gains have been spurred by expectations of lower inflation and at least one official interest rate cut before the end of the year.
